mappings.note: Asks what lesson the boy learns from losing the ball - the poet's message about loss and responsibility, LO-2.

Malformed row whose stem has swallowed a previous answer; the live question asks why the dead cow is 'ironically significant' for Valli. Irony is a literary convention that no LO in this frame names, so C-E1.4.
Describes the furniture's behaviour as narrated in 'Footprints Without Feet'. Information extraction, LO-1.
Compares the caged tiger with Custard the dragon, which means weighing what each poet does with his creature - the writers' messages, LO-2.
The facts of Anne's childhood are stated in the family sketch; retrieval, LO-1.
Anne lists her family, aunts and thirty friends in the text, so the answer is extracted rather than inferred; LO-1.
Write a debate script taking a side on reinforcement and student behaviour. Format, register and argued opinion, C-E1.2.
Compose a counsellor dialogue from a given opening. Dialogue format and tone, C-E1.2.
Choose two characters from the book who could be Anne's confidantes and analyse the traits they share - character analysis across texts, LO-2.
Both halves - the essay Mr Keesing set and Anne's argument in it - are stated in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
A pre-reading task predicting which bus-related words and phrases will occur. Word and phrase knowledge, C-E1.1.
Describe what the learner has seen from a moving bus. Personal description, C-E1.2; the story is not yet in play.
Valli's pastime of watching the street is stated in the opening; retrieval, LO-1.
The bus as her unending joy and her wish to ride it are both stated; retrieval, LO-1.
What she learned about the fare and the timings, and how she picked it up by listening, are narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
'What do you think Valli was planning' asks the reader to infer the scheme the text has not yet revealed - LO-2.
The conductor's 'madam' is gentle teasing of a child acting grown-up; explaining it means reading both characters, LO-2.
Why she stood up and what she then saw are both described in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
Valli's retort about having paid a full fare is quoted in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
Why she kept her distance from the old woman is about Valli's fastidiousness and pride - her attitude, LO-2, rather than the woman's listed features.
The saving of every coin and the pleasures given up are narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
The frightened cow running before the bus is described; retrieval, LO-1.
Her reasons for staying on the bus - no money, no knowledge of the town, the need to get home - are stated; retrieval, LO-1.
'What does this tell you about her' makes the refusal of the drink a window on her character, LO-2.
'Find the words and phrases in the story that tell you this' is an explicit evidence requirement, LO-3.
The whole plan - the fare, the timings, the slipping away - is narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
Requires the learner to fill quoted lines from the story and use them as the clues to Valli's character - evidence-based answering, LO-3.
Duplicate of the 'madam' question; explaining the conductor's teasing is character analysis, LO-2.
'Find the lines in the text which tell you' is the evidence outcome, LO-3.
Why she will not look out on the way back turns on the change the dead cow works in her - her state of mind, LO-2.
Her remark is funny only because the reader knows the secret her mother does not - dramatic irony, which is a literary convention and so C-E1.4 rather than a plain comprehension outcome.
'Can you find evidence from the text for this statement' is an explicit evidence requirement, LO-3.
Write a dialogue about what travel teaches, from a given opening. Dialogue format and opinion, C-E1.2.
A dated first-person diary entry reflecting on one's own demands. Format and personal expression, C-E1.2.
A character sketch of Valli as organised, bold and sensitive. LO-2 covers character analysis; the variant that asks for quoted sentences is the LO-3 item.
The bus with its changing passengers is named as the street's chief attraction; retrieval, LO-1.
'What can you tell about the conductor' asks the learner to judge him from how he behaves - character inference, LO-2.
The running cow is stated as the cause of her laughter; retrieval, LO-1.
The merry-go-round she gave up at the fair is named; retrieval, LO-1.
The woman's stretched earlobes and betel juice are described in the text, so the answer is a list of stated details, LO-1, while the 'why wouldn't she befriend her' item is the LO-2 one.
